cards.front: Effective Java Item 26 — what is a raw type and why avoid it?
cards.back: A generic type used without type arguments (List) — it switches off type checking
cards.extra: Raw types exist for pre-Java-5 code. Use List<Object> when you mean any element type; the raw form only loses safety.
cards.example:
class RawType {
    void f() {
        java.util.List raw = new java.util.ArrayList(); // no type arguments: checking switched off
        raw.add(Integer.valueOf(1)); raw.add("anything"); // both accepted
    }
}

cards.extra: Only the wildcard version can accept a List<String>. That distinction is why is the type for "some list".

cards.front: Effective Java Item 27 — why must you not ignore unchecked warnings?
cards.back: Each one is a potential ClassCastException at runtime
cards.extra: The compiler is telling you it could not verify a cast. Eliminate the warning, or suppress it at the smallest scope with a comment saying why it is safe.
cards.example:
class Unchecked {
    static java.util.List cast(java.util.List raw) { return raw; } // unchecked warning
    void f() { String s = cast(java.util.List.of(42)).get(0); } // potential ClassCastException later
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 28 — how do arrays and generics differ on subtyping?
cards.back: Arrays are covariant (String[] is an Object[]); generics are invariant (List<String> is not a List<Object>)
cards.extra: Array covariance is why Object[] x = new String[1]; x[0] = 1; compiles and then throws at runtime. Generics refuse it at compile time.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 28 — why can you not create a generic array?
cards.back: Generics are erased, arrays are reified — the runtime knows the array's component type and would reject the mismatch
cards.extra: So new List<String>[1] is illegal, and mixing the two produces unchecked warnings. Prefer lists to arrays in generic code.
cards.example:
class ErasureVsReified { void f(java.util.List strings) {
    System.out.println(strings.getClass() == java.util.ArrayList.class); // generic type erased
    Object[] a = new String[1]; // arrays know their component type at runtime
    try { a[0] = Integer.valueOf(1); } catch (ArrayStoreException e) {} // rejected
} }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 29 — what does favouring generic types mean in practice?
cards.back: Parameterise your own classes instead of storing Object
cards.extra: A Stack holding Object needs a cast on every pop; Stack<E> moves that check to compile time.
cards.example:
class Box {
    private T value;
    void set(T v) { value = v; } T get() { return value; } // parameterised, not Object + casts
}
class Use { void f() { Box b = new Box<>(); b.set("x"); String s = b.get(); } }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 30 — what is a generic method?
cards.back: A method that declares its own type parameters, e.g. static <E> Set<E> union(Set<E> a, Set<E> b)
cards.extra: Static utility methods usually cannot use the class's type parameter, so they declare their own. The type is inferred at the call site.
cards.example:
class GenericMethod {
    static  java.util.Set union(java.util.Set a, java.util.Set b) {
        java.util.Set r = new java.util.HashSet<>(a); r.addAll(b); return r;
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 31 — what do bounded wildcards buy you?
cards.back: API flexibility: List<? extends Number> accepts List<Integer> and List<Double>
cards.extra: Without the wildcard, one method would need one overload per element type. This is the PECS rule's 'producer extends' half.
cards.example:
java.util.List<Integer> ints = java.util.List.of(1);
java.util.List<Double> doubles = java.util.List.of(2.0);
java.util.List<? extends Number> nums = ints;
nums = doubles;   // one bounded-wildcard type accepts both

cards.front: Effective Java Item 31 — what is the PECS rule?
cards.extra: A parameter that only reads from the collection uses ? extends T; one that only writes uses ? super T. Both at once means no wildcard.
cards.example:
class Pecs {
    static  void copy(java.util.List src, java.util.List dst) {
        for (E e : src) dst.add(e); // producer extends, consumer super
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 32 — what is heap pollution with generic varargs?
cards.back: A varargs parameter is really an array, so a call can put the wrong type into it
cards.extra: @SafeVarargs is the promise that the method does not store into the array. Do not mix varargs and generics casually.
cards.example:
final class Varargs {
    @SafeVarargs static <T> void add(java.util.List<T> l, T... items) { l.add(items[0]); }
    @SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "rawtypes"})
    static void demo() { java.util.List<String> s = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); add((java.util.List) s, new Integer[]{42}); }   // polluted
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 33 — what is a typesafe heterogeneous container?
cards.back: A map keyed by Class<T>, where each key checks the value's type at insert and cast at get
cards.extra: Map<Class<?>, Object> plus casts inside put/get gives one container that holds many unrelated types safely.
cards.example:
class Hetero {
    private final java.util.Map, Object> m = new java.util.HashMap<>();
     void put(Class k, T v) { m.put(k, v); } // key checks value type at insert
     T get(Class k) { return k.cast(m.get(k)); } // checked cast at get
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 34 — why use an enum instead of int constants?
cards.back: Type safety, printable names, and the ability to iterate over all values
cards.extra: int constants are unchecked: any int is accepted, and a wrong one fails silently. An enum makes the set closed and self-describing.
cards.example:
enum Color { RED, GREEN }
class EnumBenefits { void f() {
    for (Color c : Color.values()) System.out.println(c); // printable names, all values
    Color safe = Color.RED; System.out.println(safe); // type-safe, unlike int constants
} }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 35 — why is ordinal() a bad source of an associated value?
cards.back: Reordering or inserting constants silently changes every derived number
cards.extra: Store the value in an instance field, set through a constructor. The ordinal is for internal use, never for persisted or computed data.
cards.example:
enum Priority { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH;
    int value() { return ordinal(); } // reordering/inserting silently changes derived numbers
}
class OrdinalTrap { void f() { System.out.println(Priority.HIGH.value()); } }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 37 — what replaces indexing an array by ordinal()?
cards.back: EnumMap — a map keyed by the enum constant
cards.extra: You get type safety and no dependency on declaration order, with array-like speed.
cards.example:
enum Day { MON, TUE, WED }
class Schedules {
    java.util.EnumMap plan = new java.util.EnumMap<>(Day.class);
    void f() { plan.put(Day.MON, "work"); String s = plan.get(Day.MON); } // keyed by constant, not ordinal
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 38 — how do you emulate an extensible enum?
cards.back: Define an interface and have each "extension" enum implement it
cards.extra: Enums cannot be extended by design. The interface gives callers a common type while each enum stays closed.
cards.example:
interface Op { int apply(int x); }
enum Base implements Op { INC { public int apply(int x) { return x + 1; } } }
enum Ext implements Op { DEC { public int apply(int x) { return x - 1; } } }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 39 — what is wrong with the JUnit-3 style naming convention for tests?
cards.back: A typo silently skips the test — no compile error, no failure
cards.extra: Naming patterns are checked by nothing. Annotations (@Test) make the tool's expectations explicit and verified by the compiler.
cards.example:
class JUnitNameTypo {
    void tsetSomething() {} // typo: not testXxx, so the test is silently skipped
    void testSomething() {} // the intended test; both compile without error
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 40 — what bug does @Override catch?
cards.back: A method that looks like an override but has a different signature, so it silently becomes a new method
cards.extra: The book's Bigram example: equals(Bigram) instead of equals(Object) compiles and never runs. @Override turns it into an error.
cards.example:
class Parent { void send() {} }
class Child extends Parent {
    @Override void send() {} // correct signature: real override
    // @Override void sen() {} // compile error: typo would silently add a new method
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 41 — when is a marker interface better than a marker annotation?
cards.back: When the marker should define a type — it can then be used in method signatures and checked at compile time
cards.extra: Serializable is a type; an annotation is metadata. The book's rule: use an interface if you need to write code against the property.
cards.example:
interface Marked {}
@interface Marker {}
class Use {
    void require(Marked x) {} // marker interface defines a type checked at compile time
    void annotate(@Marker Object x) {} // annotation alone is not a type
}
